title: Adaptive mini-batch merging and kernel priority
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem: Small inflight prefill/ decode windows create many tiny batches that incur per-batch kernel launch overheads and increase 99th-percentile latency. Existing admission policies reduce some noise but do not optimally merge short-lived mini-batches across low-contention lanes without harming tail latency for high-priority requests.

Goal: Implement an adaptive mini-batch merging layer in the admission path that opportunistically coalesces near-simultaneous short requests into short-lived merged batches and uses a kernel-priority heuristic to prefer kernels that reduce tail amplification for mixed-length workloads. The feature should be safe for SLO-tenanted customers and configurable by routing policy.

Scope: Admission-level merging + kernel priority weight computation, light-weight memory-safe merging buffer, metrics and dashboards, controlled canary rollout, integration with existing prefill/ decode orchestration and KV cache handling. Excludes long-term kernel autotuner changes (handled in a follow-up ticket).
proposed_solution: 1) Introduce a merging window (configurable, default 3-6ms) where short requests are buffered per-tenant lane and coalesced if they meet compatibility constraints (model, dtype, quantization profile, sequence length bucket). 2) Compute a kernel_priority score per candidate merged batch that accounts for expected kernel warmness, aggregate sequence length, and deadline slacks. 3) Prefer kernel variants with lower per-batch overhead for merged batches (e.g., fused attention kernels or single-stream kernels) while keeping a fast-fail path to the default kernel when memory/compatibility prohibits the preferred kernel. 4) Emit fine-grained metrics: merged_batch_rate, merge_success_ratio, added_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, kernel_switch_count. 5) Canary rollout by tenant tags with circuit-breaker if 99.9th latency regresses beyond threshold.
acceptance_criteria: Merged batches should reduce average per-token latency cost by >= 8% for synthetic mixed-short workloads
99th-percentile latency for high-priority lanes must not increase by more than 5ms or 10% (whichever smaller) during canary
No correctness regressions: outputs unchanged for canonical prompt suite within noise bounds
Dashboard graphs for merged_batch_rate and kernel_priority distribution exist and show expected behavior during experiment
updates: 2026-03-02: Spike complete — implemented prototype merging buffer in dev runtime. Observed 12% per-token cost reduction on 50% short/50% long synthetic mix, but saw a small P99 bump on high-priority single-shot requests when merge-window was 10ms.

2026-03-04: Narrowed default merge window to 4ms and added sequence-length bucketing; P99 regression eliminated on preliminary tests. Added kernel_priority metric and a safety gate that disables merging when KV cache miss rate > 15%.

2026-03-06: Design review with PM and Console team. PM requested tenant-level opt-out flags and a conservative default for enterprise tenants. Console team requested two dashboards: per-route merge impact and per-kernel switch costs.

2026-03-08: Running 48-hour canary on internal staging with 8 tenants (mixed workloads). Merged_batch_rate ~22% for short requests; overall token cost down 9.4%. Observed one spike correlated with an unrelated autoscaling event — flagged as non-blocking. Created PR #6482.

2026-03-10: Engineering review feedback applied: improved compatibility checks to include quantization tag and added a fail-safe to split merged batches if memory footprint estimate exceeds available GPU memory. Preparing draft runbook for canary rollback conditions.
comments: PM review (Ravi Shah): Please ensure tenant opt-out and a human-readable console explanation for when merging is active.
Design feedback (Lena Mueller): Kernel-priority heuristics look fine but add telemetry so we can correlate choices with actual kernel time reductions.
Security (Priya Nair): No new data paths introduced; confirm that merge-buffer uses existing request encryption in transit and no new persistence is added.
Infra (Owen Park): Watch for scheduler interactions during bursty ingress; merging may change observed load patterns for autoscaler.
tradeoffs: Merging introduces small extra queuing delay for short requests in exchange for lower per-token compute cost; tuned window attempts to limit added latency.
Kernel switching can reduce overhead for merged batches but increases code-path complexity and may reduce cache locality for other lanes.
Conservative defaults and tenant opt-outs needed to protect SLAs for enterprise customers.
